problem: Prior learned mapping-and-planning navigators (CMP, VIN-style) assume noise-free actuation and dense, consecutive online observations, so they never have to localize within their map. Classical pipelines instead depend on geometric relocalization at every step, which fails in featureless or changing scenes and cannot use priors from other environments. Reactive learned policies keep only implicit LSTM memory and build no usable spatial representation.
motivation: Human navigation combines two things: map-like survey knowledge for planning and shortcuts, and landmark-based visual fixes that correct drift while following a route. The authors observe that under noisy actuation, open-loop replay of a plan drifts and compounding errors grow. A plan is therefore more useful if it also says what the agent should expect to see along the way. Because every module is learned, the system can use statistical priors from other buildings and still work from only a handful of sparse registered views.
key_idea: Plan on a learned allocentric map built from a few sparse posed RGB images, then compile the plan into a 'path signature' of (action, pose, synthesized expected features) tuples. A learned recurrent controller follows this signature with a sequential soft-attention pointer, using the landmark features as visual fixes to correct noisy actuation without explicit relocalization or replanning.
insight: Explicit visual memory in the form of synthesized landmark features, read by a structured sequential-attention policy, is what makes plan following robust. With all path images available, the proposed policy reaches 80.5% success versus 43.2% for a vanilla GRU given the same memories and 35.7% for a learned executor without visual memory. With only 40 random environment images it still beats the no-memory baseline (37.4 vs 35.7). A differentiable nearest-neighbor matcher over the signature reaches 84% with all path images but collapses to 5–12% with subsets, showing that feature synthesis plus learned attention is needed when memories are sparse. Two practical findings: a shallow 5-layer strided CNN beat ImageNet ResNet features, which the authors attribute to pose-sensitive features being easier to learn; and an auxiliary loss with a curriculum from real to synthesized features aided training.
method: Learned mapper: each sparse posed RGB image goes through a conv encoder ψ, FC layers g and an upconv decoder φ to give an egocentric top-view feature map (unconstrained features, not strictly free space). A differentiable spatial transformer warps it into the allocentric frame using the image pose θ_i. The maps are fused by weighted averaging Σ_m and upsampled by deconvolutions U.

Learned planner: value iteration expressed as a conv net with channel max-pooling (VIN), trained jointly with the mapper (CMP-style) to output optimal actions at every map cell. The full action sequence and the corresponding pose sequence are read off by following argmax actions from start to goal.

Feature synthesizer: for each planned pose ρ_j, each reference image's feature ψ(I_i) is fused with its relative pose δ(θ_i, ρ_j) by a network Ω. The contributions are combined by weighted addition Σ_f into a hallucinated feature f̂_j for a location the agent may never have visited.
Path signature: the sequence of tuples (a_j, ρ_j, f̂_j) encoding the planned actions, poses and expected observations along the path.

Plan-execution policy: a recurrent net reads the signature through soft attention centered at a pointer η, with weights e^{-|η−j|}. At each step it takes the attended signature, the current RGB feature and its hidden state, and outputs an action plus a pointer increment (η_{t+1} = η_t + sigmoid(·)), acting as a closed-loop controller that corrects drift.

Training: the policy is trained with DAgger imitation of optimal actions from the true simulator state. An auxiliary loss ties synthesized features to real features, with a gradual switch from real to synthesized features when building signatures. Images are encoded by a 5-layer strided CNN, and training uses Adam for 60K iterations.

setting.backbone: Custom shallow 5-layer strided CNN image encoder + CMP-style mapper and value-iteration planner + attention-based recurrent (GRU-style) policy, all trained from scratch
setting.training_data: Stanford Large-Scale 3D Indoor Spaces (S3DIS) areas 1, 5 and 6, rendered with the adapted CMP simulator (area 3 for validation). Policy trained by DAgger imitation of optimal actions; mapper and planner supervised with optimal actions (or free space in the isolated mapping study). No extra or web data.
setting.observation: Egocentric monocular RGB (60° FOV), plus a sparse set of registered reference RGB images with known poses, and the start and goal poses
setting.action_space: 4 discrete actions: stay, rotate left 90°, rotate right 90°, forward 40 cm; the forward action fails with 20% probability (agent stays in place)
setting.simulator: Gupta et al. (CMP) simulator over S3DIS textured meshes
setting.privileged: Poses of the reference images and start and goal poses are given. In the path-following experiments (Table 1) the optimal plan (actions and poses) is supplied as an oracle. Training supervision uses the true simulator state.

numbers_note: Several results appear only in Figure 4 plots and have no printed numbers: mapper free-space AP versus number of images, open-loop planning success versus number of images, feature-synthesis localization AP versus a SIFT baseline, and final distance-to-goal distributions for longer 32–36-step goals. The text reports some extra figures: 73% vs 80% success with perturbed input images; nearest-neighbor executor at 84% with all path images but 5–12% with subsets; planning success of about 70% in the full-system setting (Table 2 open-loop no-noise row: 69.53 SR). The benchmark is custom: S3DIS area 4 test building, 8K sampled episodes for Table 1, with no official episode set. The text calls the environments 'Matterport scans', but the dataset is S3DIS.
results: When executing a given optimal plan under 20% forward-action failure, the path-signature policy reaches 80.5% success with all path images. This beats a vanilla GRU given the same memories (43.2%), a learned executor without visual memory (35.7%) and open-loop replay (26.9%). With only 40 random environment images it still reaches 37.4%, above the no-memory learned executor (35.7%). In the full system, where the plan comes from the learned mapper and planner using 40 random images, it reaches 26.90% success (mean DTG 6.86). This is only marginally above learned plan execution (26.65%) and above open-loop execution (20.34%); open-loop plans with no noise succeed 69.53% of the time.
limitations: Full-system gains are marginal (26.90 vs 26.65 success), and planning quality from sparse views (about 70% noise-free success) bounds end-to-end performance. Most gains are shown only with oracle optimal plans.

Toy setting: discrete 90° turns and 40 cm steps, noise modeled only as forward-action failure, short horizons (16–18 steps, 20-step budget), and a single test building. No real-robot or continuous-action experiments (the authors list these as future work).
Requires accurately posed (registered) reference images and known start and goal poses. Much of the evaluation is factored module by module rather than end to end.
